items: 1. 51% Majority Attack : Allows an adversary controlling majority hash-rate to double-spend their own recent transactions and censor competing blocks, without acquiring the cryptographic ability to forge digital signatures of other users' cold wallets
2. Sybil Attack : Monopolizing all incoming and outgoing peer-to-peer connections of a single targeted validator node to isolate it from the honest network and feed it a fabricated ledger state
3. Eclipse Attack : A single malicious operator spinning up thousands of pseudonymous node identities across the network to gain disproportionate influence over network voting or routing

4. Replay Attack : Intercepting a cryptographically valid signed transaction broadcasted on one blockchain and maliciously re-broadcasting it onto a newly hard-forked chain where the same signature parameters remain valid
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: A 51% consensus attack compromises transaction ordering and finality (enabling double-spending of the attacker's own coins) but cannot break asymmetric public-key cryptography to steal arbitrary cold-wallet funds; Sybil attacks flood the network as a whole with fake identities, whereas Eclipse attacks isolate one specific target node.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Controlling over 50% of a network's mining hash-rate (in Proof-of-Work) or validating stake allows an attacker to rewrite recent block history (reorg) to reverse their own spent transactions (double-spending) and block other transactions from being included. However, majority hash-rate does not break Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithms (ECDSA) or SHA-256; hence, the attacker cannot forge signatures to spend coins belonging to other users' uncompromised wallets.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. Surrounding a single specific target node by monopolizing all of its peer-to-peer neighbour slots so that it only communicates with attacker-controlled nodes is an Eclipse Attack, not a broad Sybil Attack.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Creating a multitude of fake, pseudonymous identities by a single entity to subvert reputation systems or peer routing across a distributed network is a Sybil Attack (which Proof-of-Work and Proof-of-Stake are specifically designed to make economically costly).

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Following a contentious hard fork (where two chains share identical transaction history and address keys up to the split block), a signed transaction intended for Chain A can be copied and re-broadcasted ('replayed') by an attacker on Chain B unless unique Chain IDs (replay protection, such as EIP-155) are embedded inside the signed payload.

ref: NIST Internal Report (NISTIR 8202) Blockchain Technology Overview

stem: Consider the following statements regarding secure communication protocols:
items: Statement-I: In cryptographic protocols implementing Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS), the theft or compromise of a party's long-term private key at a future date does not enable an adversary to decrypt previously recorded ciphertext sessions.

Statement-II: In End-to-End Encryption (E2EE) messaging architectures, intermediary telecom and application servers only route encrypted ciphertext payloads and do not possess the private decryption keys held by the communicating endpoints.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While End-to-End Encryption (E2EE) prevents intermediary servers from reading data in transit, Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) specifically requires Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange so that unique session keys are discarded after each conversation, protecting historical traffic even if an endpoint's long-term private key is later compromised.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS), mandated in modern protocols such as TLS 1.3 and the Signal Double Ratchet protocol, ensures that even if an adversary records encrypted traffic today and later steals the server's or user's long-term private key, none of the past sessions can be retroactively decrypted.

Statement-II is also correct, as E2EE ensures that cryptographic keys reside only at the communicating endpoints rather than on intermediary routing servers. However, Statement-II does NOT explain Statement-I: if an E2EE system relied on a static RSA private key at the endpoint to encrypt session keys directly, stealing that endpoint's long-term private key in the future would expose all past recorded communications. Statement-I is explained instead by Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE/ECDHE) key exchange, which negotiates temporary, single-use session keys that are permanently deleted from memory as soon as the session ends.

ref: IETF RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3 Specification); Signal Cryptographic Protocol Documentation

stem: Consider the following architectural stages in the lifecycle of a standard public blockchain transaction from initiation to ledger finality:
items: 1. Verification of the digital signature by block-producing nodes and aggregation of selected transactions into a candidate block's Merkle Tree
2. Hashing the raw transaction payload and signing the message digest locally using the sender's private key inside the wallet client
3. Execution of the network consensus mechanism (Proof-of-Work or Proof-of-Stake) and propagation of the validated block to append it to the canonical chain
4. Broadcasting the signed transaction across the peer-to-peer gossip network and staging it in the unconfirmed Memory Pool (Mempool)
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of the stages given above?
core: A public blockchain transaction progresses sequentially from local client-side hashing and private-key signing (Step 2), to peer-to-peer broadcast into the unconfirmed Mempool (Step 4), to miner/validator selection and Merkle Tree block assembly (Step 1), and finally to consensus execution and canonical chain inclusion (Step 3).

exp.why: Stage 1 is the third chronological step: miners or validators pull pending unconfirmed transactions out of their Mempool (commonly prioritizing higher gas/transaction fees), verify their public-key signatures and account balances, and hash them pairwise into a candidate block's Merkle Tree.

Stage 2 is the first chronological step: before any network communication occurs, the user's local wallet software constructs the transaction data, computes its cryptographic hash digest, and signs it locally using the sender's private key.

Stage 3 is the fourth and final chronological step: once the candidate block is assembled with its Merkle Root in the header, the network executes Proof-of-Work (nonce hashing) or Proof-of-Stake (proposer attestation), and the winning block is propagated to all full nodes to update the canonical ledger state.

Stage 4 is the second chronological step: immediately after local signing (Stage 2), the wallet broadcasts the signed transaction to connected nodes via the peer-to-peer gossip protocol, where it waits in the Memory Pool (Mempool) of unconfirmed transactions before being picked up for candidate block construction (Stage 1). Option A represents a procedural trap (T6) by placing candidate block Merkle Tree assembly before Mempool entry.

ref: NCERT Class XII Computer Science (Emerging Trends); Mastering Blockchain Architecture

stem: In the context of Artificial Intelligence architectures, which one of the following best describes the fundamental distinction between classical Machine Learning algorithms (such as Support Vector Machines or Decision Trees) and Deep Learning networks?

opts.A: Classical Machine Learning algorithms operate exclusively on labeled datasets, whereas Deep Learning networks operate exclusively on unlabeled datasets without human supervision.
opts.B: Classical Machine Learning algorithms adjust synaptic weights using multi-layer backpropagation, whereas Deep Learning networks rely on predefined deterministic if-then heuristics.
opts.C: Deep Learning networks automatically learn hierarchical feature representations directly from raw data across multiple layers, whereas classical Machine Learning typically relies on human domain experts for manual feature engineering.
opts.D: Deep Learning networks require significantly smaller training datasets and lower computational overhead to converge compared to classical Machine Learning algorithms.

core: The defining architectural advancement of Deep Learning over classical Machine Learning is automated representation learning (feature extraction) across stacked neural layers, eliminating the bottleneck of manual feature engineering by domain experts.

exp.why: Option C is correct because classical Machine Learning algorithms (like Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, or Logistic Regression) generally require structured inputs where human domain experts have manually identified, extracted, and engineered the relevant features (e.g., edge ratios, pixel histograms, or domain variables). In contrast, Deep Learning utilizes multi-layered Artificial Neural Networks to perform automated representation learning—extracting low-level features in initial layers (such as edges or acoustic frequencies) and progressively composing them into high-level abstract concepts in deeper layers directly from raw unstructured data. Option A is incorrect (T3 conflation trap) because both classical Machine Learning and Deep Learning can be trained under supervised (labeled), unsupervised (unlabeled), or reinforcement paradigms. Option B is incorrect because multi-layer backpropagation of synaptic weights is the hallmark of Deep Learning, not classical rule-based heuristics. Option D is incorrect because Deep Learning typically requires vastly larger datasets and high-performance parallel computing hardware (GPUs/TPUs) to optimize millions or billions of parameters without overfitting.

ref: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, Deep Learning (MIT Press), Ch. 1; NCERT Class XII Computer Science / MeitY National AI Portal

stem: With reference to the training paradigms used in modern Artificial Intelligence and Foundation Models, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In Self-Supervised Learning, a model generates its own supervisory signals directly from raw unlabeled data by masking or withholding parts of the input and learning to predict the missing segments.

2. The initial pre-training phase of Large Language Models across massive internet-scale text corpora relies primarily on manually annotated human labels under a strictly supervised learning paradigm.
3. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is a data-preprocessing technique applied prior to pre-training in order to compress and deduplicate the raw training dataset.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Foundation models overcome the human data-labeling bottleneck by using Self-Supervised Learning during massive initial pre-training, followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and post-training alignment via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) is a paradigm where the model extracts supervisory signals automatically from the structure of unlabeled data itself—for instance, hiding the next word (causal language modeling in GPT) or masking random tokens inside a sentence (masked language modeling in BERT) and training the neural network to predict the hidden tokens from the surrounding context.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Manually labeling trillions of words across internet-scale corpora is practically impossible. Therefore, the initial pre-training phase of Large Language Models relies on Self-Supervised Learning over unlabeled text, whereas human-annotated Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is used only in a later stage on much smaller, curated instruction datasets.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is not a pre-training data compression technique; it is a post-training alignment stage applied after pre-training and supervised fine-tuning. In RLHF, human evaluators rank alternative model responses to train a reward model, which then optimizes the language model's policy to be helpful, honest, and harmless.

ref: Stanford HAI Foundation Models Report; IndiaAI Mission Technical Compendium

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the mathematical mechanics of Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs):
items: Statement-I: Deep neural networks incorporate non-linear activation functions (such as ReLU or Sigmoid) between layers because, without non-linearity, a multi-layer neural network mathematically collapses into an equivalent single-layer linear transformation regardless of its depth.

Statement-II: During the training of an Artificial Neural Network, the backpropagation algorithm applies the chain rule of calculus to iteratively adjust synaptic weights in proportion to the gradient of the loss function.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Non-linear activation functions prevent deep networks from algebraically collapsing into a single linear transformation, while backpropagation uses the calculus chain rule to propagate error gradients backward for weight optimization.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Every layer in a neural network computes a weighted linear sum of its inputs plus a bias (y = Wx + b). By the fundamental laws of linear algebra, the composition of any number of linear transformations is itself strictly a single linear transformation (W2(W1*x) = W_effective*x). Thus, without inserting a non-linear activation function (like Rectified Linear Unit [ReLU], Sigmoid, or Tanh) between layers, even a 100-layer network could never approximate non-linear decision boundaries and would collapse into a single-layer linear model.

Statement-II is correct. Backpropagation is the core optimization mechanism that computes the partial derivative (gradient) of the network's loss function with respect to each synaptic weight by applying the chain rule of differential calculus backward from the output layer to the input layer. However, Statement-II describes how weights are updated during training and does not explain why composing linear layers without non-linear activation functions algebraically collapses into a single linear transformation.

ref: Goodfellow et al., Deep Learning, Ch. 6 (Deep Feedforward Networks); Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning

stem: With reference to specialized Deep Learning architectures and their core operational mechanisms, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) : Applies sliding spatial filters (kernels) and pooling layers to capture local translation-invariant hierarchies in grid-like visual data
2. Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) : Maintains an internal hidden state through cyclic feedback connections to process sequential and time-series data
3. Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) : Synthesizes new media by learning to iteratively reverse the gradual addition of Gaussian noise to training samples
4. Diffusion Model : Trains two competing neural networks simultaneously in a zero-sum minimax game where one generates synthetic samples and the other attempts to detect them
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: CNNs extract spatial hierarchies via convolution kernels and RNNs track temporal sequences via cyclic hidden states; in generative AI, GANs pit a Generator against a Discriminator in a minimax game, whereas Diffusion Models iteratively denoise Gaussian noise.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) utilize shared-weight spatial filters (convolution kernels) that slide across 2D or 3D grid data (such as images) along with pooling layers, enabling translation invariance and hierarchical detection of edges, textures, and objects.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, feature recurrent loops that pass a hidden state vector from one time step to the next, serving as short-term memory for sequential data like speech or time series.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Learning to generate synthetic media by iteratively reversing a forward process that gradually adds Gaussian noise to data is the defining mechanism of Diffusion Models (such as Stable Diffusion or Sora), not Generative Adversarial Networks.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. Training two neural networks—a Generator and a Discriminator—against each other in a zero-sum minimax game is the core architecture of a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), introduced by Ian Goodfellow, not a Diffusion Model.

ref: Goodfellow et al. (2014) Generative Adversarial Nets; Ho et al. (2020) Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models

stem: With reference to the Transformer architecture, which forms the backbone of modern Large Language Models, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Through the self-attention mechanism, a Transformer dynamically computes relevance weights between any pair of tokens in a sequence regardless of the distance separating them.
2. Like Recurrent Neural Networks, the Transformer encoder processes input tokens sequentially one after another during the training phase to preserve word order.

3. Unlike Recurrent Neural Networks that pass hidden states across sequential time steps, a standard Transformer relies only on attention mechanisms and positional encodings without using recurrent or convolutional layers to model sequence dependencies.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Transformer architecture eliminates sequential recurrence in favor of multi-head self-attention and positional encodings, enabling massive parallelization during training and direct modeling of long-range token dependencies.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The self-attention mechanism maps each token into Query, Key, and Value vectors, allowing the model to compute attention scores between every token and every other token in the context window directly in a single step, overcoming the vanishing gradient and long-range memory degradation seen in older sequential models.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Unlike Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) which must process tokens sequentially one-by-one (step t after step t-1), the Transformer encoder ingests and processes all tokens of an input sequence simultaneously in parallel during training. To preserve word order without sequential processing, it injects mathematical 'positional encodings' into the input embeddings.

Statement 3 is correct. As established in the seminal 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need', the standard Transformer architecture dispenses entirely with recurrence and convolutions, relying only on attention mechanisms coupled with positional encodings (and point-wise feed-forward layers) to capture global dependencies between inputs and outputs.

ref: Vaswani et al. (2017), 'Attention Is All You Need'; MeitY IndiaAI Technical Reports

stem: With reference to the internal working mechanics of Large Language Models (LLMs), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Model parameters, such as the learning rate and batch size, are external configuration variables set manually by engineers prior to training, whereas hyperparameters are the internal synaptic weights adjusted automatically during training.
2. In subword tokenization algorithms used by modern Large Language Models, every single token corresponds strictly to one complete standalone dictionary word.
3. Lowering the sampling temperature of a Large Language Model during inference makes its output probability distribution sharper and more deterministic, thereby reducing creative randomness.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: In LLMs, subword tokenization splits text into variable word fragments, internal weights/biases are 'parameters' learned automatically while external training settings are 'hyperparameters', and sampling temperature controls output stochasticity during inference.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect because it swaps the definitions of parameters and hyperparameters. 'Model parameters' (often numbering in the billions or trillions in LLMs) are the internal synaptic weights and biases learned and updated automatically by optimization algorithms during training. 'Hyperparameters' (such as learning rate, batch size, number of transformer layers, and context length) are external configuration variables set prior to the training process.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Modern LLMs use subword tokenization algorithms (such as Byte-Pair Encoding [BPE] or WordPiece) rather than strict word-level tokenization. Depending on frequency, a single token may represent a complete common word, a subword root/prefix/suffix, a single character, a punctuation mark, or a numerical digit.

Statement 3 is correct. During inference, an LLM outputs raw scores (logits) that are converted into a probability distribution over the vocabulary using the softmax function scaled by a 'temperature' parameter. Lowering the temperature (approaching 0) amplifies the probability of the highest-scoring token (greedy/deterministic decoding), making responses factual and repeatable, whereas raising the temperature flattens the distribution, increasing diversity and creative randomness.

ref: Jurafsky & Martin, Speech and Language Processing (Stanford University), Ch. 10 (Transformers and Large Language Models)

stem: With reference to the architecture and deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs), consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) eliminates factual hallucinations in Large Language Models by permanently updating the underlying neural network weights through backpropagation during each user query.

Statement-II: Standard Large Language Models generate plausible-sounding factual fabrications because they operate through autoregressive probabilistic next-token prediction rather than deterministic database lookup, and RAG mitigates this at inference time by injecting retrieved external text into the prompt context without altering model weights.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Large Language Models (LLMs) hallucinate because their transformer decoders predict the statistically most probable next token rather than querying a verified factual database. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds LLM outputs at inference time by retrieving relevant external documents and appending them to the prompt context window without modifying the frozen parameters (weights) of the neural network.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect because Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a non-parametric inference-time technique, not a training or fine-tuning process. RAG does not perform backpropagation or permanently alter the neural network's synaptic weights during a user query; modifying weights requires computationally expensive Model Fine-Tuning (such as Supervised Fine-Tuning or LoRA).

Statement-II is correct. Pre-trained LLMs compress training corpus statistics into high-dimensional parameter weights and generate text autoregressively by sampling the conditional probability distribution of the next token. Because they lack an intrinsic truth-verification mechanism, they can synthesize fluent falsehoods (hallucinations). RAG mitigates this by fetching verified domain documents from an external vector database and feeding them directly into the model's context window as reference material.

ref: MeitY IndiaAI Mission Technical Reports; NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (Generative AI Profile)

stem: With reference to optimization techniques used for deploying Artificial Intelligence (AI) models on resource-constrained Edge hardware such as smartphones and IoT sensors, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Model Quantization reduces inference latency on edge devices by converting low-precision 8-bit integer weights into higher-precision 32-bit floating-point representations.

2. In Knowledge Distillation, a compact 'student' model is trained first on local device data and subsequently transfers its learned probability distributions to train a larger, cloud-based 'teacher' model.
3. Weight Pruning compresses a deep neural network by dynamically inserting additional convolutional layers during real-time edge inference.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Deploying deep neural networks on edge Neural Processing Units (NPUs) requires model compression via Quantization (reducing numerical bit-width), Pruning (removing redundant low-magnitude weights/connections), and Knowledge Distillation (training a compact student model to mimic a large pre-trained teacher model).

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect because Model Quantization works in the exact opposite direction: it reduces the numerical precision of neural network weights and activations from high-precision formats like 32-bit or 16-bit floating-point (FP32/FP16) down to lower-precision formats such as 8-bit or 4-bit integers (INT8/INT4). This drastically cuts memory bandwidth usage, power consumption, and arithmetic latency on edge hardware.

Statement 2 is incorrect because it reverses the roles in Knowledge Distillation. In Knowledge Distillation, a large, computationally heavy 'teacher' model is trained first, and its rich output probability distributions ('soft targets') are used to supervise and train a much smaller, lightweight 'student' model that can run efficiently on edge devices.

Statement 3 is incorrect because Weight Pruning compresses a model by systematically eliminating (setting to zero or removing) redundant, near-zero synaptic weights, neurons, or attention heads that contribute minimally to output accuracy, rather than adding convolutional layers during inference.

ref: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems; MeitY Edge AI & NPU Architecture Briefs

stem: In the context of advanced computing hardware architectures, consider the following statements comparing Neuromorphic Computing with conventional Von Neumann Computing:
items: 1. Unlike conventional Von Neumann architectures that incur heavy energy costs shuttling data between physically separated processing and memory units, neuromorphic processors co-locate memory and computation within artificial synaptic cores.
2. Neuromorphic chips achieve superior power efficiency by driving all artificial neurons across the silicon die via a continuous, high-frequency synchronous global clock bus.

3. Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) executed on neuromorphic hardware encode information using the precise temporal timing and frequency of discrete voltage spikes rather than continuous synchronous matrix multiplications.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Neuromorphic processors overcome the 'Von Neumann bottleneck' by mimicking biological brains through in-memory synaptic computation and event-driven, asynchronous Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), consuming power only when sparse neural spikes occur.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Classical CPUs and GPUs follow the Von Neumann architecture, where the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) and memory bank reside in separate regions connected by a data bus, creating the energy-intensive 'Von Neumann bottleneck'. Neuromorphic chips integrate memory and processing within distributed neuro-synaptic cores (often using memristors or localized SRAM), closely mirroring biological synapses.

Statement 2 is incorrect. A defining feature of neuromorphic architecture is that it is event-driven and asynchronous, eliminating the power-hungry global clock tree of conventional synchronous processors. Individual artificial neurons remain idle and draw negligible power until incoming signals push their membrane potential past a firing threshold.

Statement 3 is correct. While conventional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) rely on dense, clock-synchronized floating-point matrix multiplications, Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) on neuromorphic hardware process sparse, discrete binary spikes over time, encoding rich spatio-temporal information in spike timing and inter-spike intervals.

ref: DST National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber-Physical Systems (NM-ICPS); Nature Electronics Reviews on Neuromorphic Hardware

stem: In a quantum processor, a qubit is prepared in a coherent state of quantum superposition of its two computational basis states (|0⟩ and |1⟩). When an external measurement apparatus directly reads the state of this single qubit, what physically occurs?
prompt: Select the correct answer from the options given below:

opts.A: The detector outputs a continuous fractional voltage representing the exact mathematical average of both 0 and 1 simultaneously.
opts.B: The quantum superposition irreversibly collapses, yielding a single definite classical outcome of either 0 or 1 with probabilities governed by the squared magnitudes of its complex amplitudes.
opts.C: The qubit splits into two independent classical bits, allowing the readout register to store both 0 and 1 in parallel from a single measurement.
opts.D: The measurement leaves the coherent superposition completely undisturbed while copying the complex phase amplitudes into a classical memory register.

core: While an isolated qubit evolves as a coherent linear combination of basis states α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ prior to observation, projective quantum measurement induces wave-function collapse, yielding only a single classical bit (either 0 with probability |α|² or 1 with probability |β|²).

exp.why: Option (B) is correct. By the Born rule of quantum mechanics, a qubit in superposition |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ (where |α|² + |β|² = 1) exists in a coherent linear combination of states only while isolated from environmental decoherence and measurement. The act of measurement forces the wave function to project (collapse) stochastically onto one of the orthogonal basis eigenstates, producing a single classical bit—either 0 (with probability |α|²) or 1 (with probability |β|²). Option (A) and (C) are false because a single qubit measurement can extract at most one classical bit of information (Holevo's bound) and never outputs both values simultaneously. Option (D) violates both wave-function collapse principles and the Quantum No-Cloning Theorem.

ref: National Quantum Mission (NQM) DST Primers; Nielsen & Chuang, Quantum Computation and Quantum Information

stem: With reference to Quantum Entanglement and relativistic limits on information transfer, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Although measuring one qubit of a quantum-entangled pair instantaneously fixes the correlated quantum state of its partner regardless of spatial separation, quantum entanglement alone cannot be used to transmit classical messages faster than the speed of light.

Statement-II: According to the quantum No-Communication Theorem, the local measurement of an individual entangled qubit produces a fundamentally random outcome, so any non-local correlation or encoded message can only be decoded after comparing observations through a classical communication channel constrained by the speed of light.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Quantum entanglement exhibits instantaneous non-local state correlations across arbitrary distances (Bell non-locality), but the No-Communication Theorem prevents superluminal signaling because local measurement outcomes remain completely stochastic until partnered with a light-speed-limited classical communication channel.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. When two qubits share an entangled Bell state, measuring the spin or polarization of the first qubit instantaneously determines the correlated state of the second qubit even across astronomical distances. However, this non-local wave-function collapse does not violate Einstein's Special Relativity because no controllable classical signal or usable information travels faster than light in vacuum.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Under the Quantum No-Communication Theorem, the reduced density matrix of the distant observer's qubit is unaffected by whatever local unitary operation or measurement the sender performs. The receiver sees only a 50:50 random sequence of 0s and 1s locally; even in protocols like Quantum Teleportation, reconstructing the quantum state requires the sender to transmit two classical bits over a conventional channel (optical fiber or radio link) that cannot exceed the speed of light.

ref: Nobel Prize in Physics Scientific Background on Bell Inequalities & Entangled Photons; DST National Quantum Mission

stem: With reference to the mathematical foundations of Quantum Logic Gates and Quantum Algorithms, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike classical logic gates such as AND and NAND which are mathematically reversible, all unitary quantum logic gates are inherently irreversible and dissipate information at every computational step.
2. While Grover's quantum algorithm provides an exponential speedup for prime factorization of large integers, Shor's algorithm provides only a quadratic speedup for searching an unsorted database.

3. Quantum algorithms isolate the correct solution by using constructive interference to amplify erroneous computational paths while cancelling out the target solution state through destructive interference.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Quantum computation relies on reversible unitary logic gates that preserve quantum phase coherence, coupled with carefully engineered quantum interference (constructive interference for target states, destructive interference for erroneous states) to achieve exponential speedup in algebraic factoring (Shor's algorithm) and quadratic speedup in unstructured search (Grover's algorithm).

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect because it reverses the reversibility of classical and quantum gates. Classical logic gates like AND, OR, and NAND are many-to-one mappings and are inherently irreversible (you cannot uniquely deduce the two input bits from a single output bit, which causes thermodynamic heat dissipation under Landauer's principle). Conversely, because closed quantum evolution is governed by unitary operators (U†U = I), every unitary quantum logic gate (such as Hadamard, CNOT, and Toffoli gates) is strictly reversible prior to measurement.

Statement 2 is incorrect because it swaps Shor's and Grover's algorithms. Shor's algorithm achieves an exponential speedup over the best known classical algorithms for prime factorization and discrete logarithms (posing a direct threat to RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography). Grover's algorithm uses amplitude amplification to search an unstructured database of N items in O(√N) steps instead of O(N) steps, which is a quadratic (not exponential) speedup.

Statement 3 is incorrect because quantum algorithms manipulate phase amplitudes so that erroneous computational paths cancel each other out via destructive interference, whereas the probability amplitude of the correct target solution is reinforced and amplified via constructive interference so that it is observed with high probability upon measurement.

ref: NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards; National Quantum Mission (NQM) Technical Framework

stem: With reference to the physical hardware realizations of qubits and the phenomenon of quantum decoherence, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Quantum decoherence occurs when qubits interact unintentionally with thermal, electromagnetic, or vibrational disturbances in their surroundings, causing a premature loss of superposition and entanglement.

2. Photonic qubits based on light polarization require cooling to near absolute zero inside millikelvin dilution refrigerators to prevent thermal decoherence, whereas superconducting Josephson junction qubits process quantum states natively at room temperature.

3. Trapped-ion quantum processors suspend charged atomic particles in electromagnetic fields under ultra-high vacuum and manipulate their quantum states using precision lasers, typically achieving longer coherence times than superconducting qubits.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Different physical qubit modalities trade off gate speed, scalability, and thermal sensitivity: superconducting Josephson junctions require millikelvin dilution refrigerators to maintain zero electrical resistance and suppress thermal noise, whereas photonic qubits travel as light modes that barely interact with thermal environments at room temperature.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Quantum states are extraordinarily fragile; any unintended coupling between a qubit and its external environment (stray magnetic fields, thermal phonons, or cosmic radiation) acts as an implicit measurement that collapses superposition and destroys phase coherence—a process known as quantum decoherence.

Statement 2 is incorrect because it swaps the thermal operating regimes of superconducting and photonic qubits. Superconducting qubits (constructed using non-linear Josephson junctions) must be cooled to around 10–20 millikelvins inside multistage dilution refrigerators so that aluminium or niobium circuits remain superconducting and ambient thermal energy (kT) stays well below the qubit transition energy. Conversely, photonic qubits (encoding quantum information in the polarization, path, or time-bin of photons) do not couple significantly to room-temperature thermal phonons in waveguides or free space, allowing core quantum optical processing at room temperature (though single-photon superconducting nanowire detectors may still require cryogenic cooling).

Statement 3 is correct. Trapped-ion architectures (using ions such as Ytterbium-171 or Barium-133 confined in Paul or Penning electromagnetic traps inside ultra-high vacuum chambers) encode qubits in stable internal atomic hyperfine or optical levels manipulated via laser pulses. Because isolated atoms in vacuum are far better shielded from solid-state substrate defects than fabricated superconducting circuits, trapped-ion qubits exhibit coherence times ranging from seconds to minutes, though their physical logic gate speeds are slower than nanosecond-scale superconducting gates.

ref: National Quantum Mission (NQM) DST Technical Brief; Nielsen & Chuang, Quantum Computation and Quantum Information, Ch. 7

stem: Consider the following statements regarding Quantum Error Correction (QEC):
items: Statement-I: Unlike classical computers that protect data through simple bit duplication, a fault-tolerant quantum computer requires hundreds or thousands of noisy physical qubits entangled together to realize a single error-corrected logical qubit.

Statement-II: The quantum No-Cloning Theorem fundamentally prohibits the creation of identical, independent copies of an arbitrary unknown quantum state, and directly measuring a qubit to check for errors immediately collapses its superposition.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Quantum Error Correction cannot rely on classical repetition coding (copying a bit as 000 or 111 and taking a majority vote) because the No-Cloning Theorem forbids copying unknown quantum states and direct measurement destroys superposition; instead, quantum information must be distributed non-locally across large entangled arrays of physical qubits using syndrome measurements.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Present-day Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) processors suffer from high gate and decoherence error rates (around 0.1% to 1% per operation), whereas classical transistors have negligible error rates. To run deep algorithms reliably, quantum architectures must use surface codes or topological codes that entangle hundreds to thousands of physical data and ancilla qubits to construct a single fault-tolerant 'logical qubit'.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Because of the linearity of unitary quantum evolution, the No-Cloning Theorem proves that no quantum operation can duplicate an unknown arbitrary state |psi> into |psi>|psi>. Furthermore, unlike classical bits that can be inspected non-destructively at any time, measuring a data qubit directly collapses its continuous amplitude and phase (both bit-flip and phase-flip channels). Consequently, QEC must use indirect parity/syndrome measurements via auxiliary (ancilla) qubits across a vast entangled grid of physical qubits without ever reading the logical state itself.

ref: Nielsen & Chuang, Quantum Computation and Quantum Information, Ch. 10 (Quantum Error Correction)

stem: With reference to the architectural paradigms of Quantum Computing, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Quantum annealers are universal, general-purpose quantum computers specifically designed to execute sequential logic-circuit algorithms such as Shor's algorithm to factorize large integers and break RSA encryption, whereas gate-based quantum computers are restricted to solving combinatorial optimization problems.

2. Quantum annealing operates by initializing a system of qubits in a simple ground state and gradually evolving its energy landscape so that quantum tunneling guides the hardware into the lowest-energy configuration corresponding to the optimal solution of a mapped problem.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Gate-based quantum computers are universal systems that manipulate qubits through discrete, reversible unitary logic gates to run arbitrary quantum algorithms (including Shor's and Grover's), whereas quantum annealers are specialized analog-like heuristic processors designed exclusively to find global minima in discrete combinatorial optimization problems.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect because it reverses the capabilities of Universal Gate-based Quantum Computers and Quantum Annealers. Universal gate-based quantum computers apply sequential quantum logic gates (such as Hadamard, CNOT, and Phase gates) and are required to execute general-purpose circuit algorithms like Shor's integer-factorization algorithm (which threatens RSA/ECC cryptography) or Grover's search algorithm. Quantum annealers are non-universal, specialized machines restricted solely to discrete combinatorial optimization and sampling problems (such as portfolio optimization, traffic routing, or Ising spin glass models) and cannot execute Shor's algorithm.

Statement 2 is correct. Grounded in the adiabatic theorem of quantum mechanics, a quantum annealer encodes an optimization objective function into the physical interactions (couplers and biases) of an Ising Hamiltonian. By starting in an easily prepared superposition ground state and slowly morphing the system Hamiltonian toward the problem Hamiltonian, quantum tunneling allows the system to pass through narrow, high energy barriers rather than getting trapped in local minima like classical simulated annealing.

ref: DST National Quantum Mission Framework; Hidary, Quantum Computing: An Applied Approach

stem: With reference to the security mechanics of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), consider the following statements:
items: 1. In a QKD deployment such as the BB84 protocol, the entire confidential message payload is directly encoded into polarized single photons and transmitted over the quantum channel, eliminating the need for any classical communication channel or symmetric encryption algorithm.

2. Unlike Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), the security of QKD relies on the computational complexity of factoring large prime numbers and solving high-dimensional lattice problems rather than the physical properties of quantum mechanics.

3. Because quantum entanglement creates instantaneous correlations across arbitrary distances, entanglement-based QKD protocols physically prevent an eavesdropper from intercepting photons in transit and enable secret keys to be transmitted faster than the speed of light.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is used only to generate and distribute random symmetric secret keys between parties—not to transmit the actual confidential payload—and its security rests on detecting eavesdropping-induced quantum state perturbations (via Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle and the No-Cloning Theorem) rather than mathematical complexity or superluminal signaling.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. QKD is used only to generate and establish a shared random secret symmetric key between two communicating parties (Alice and Bob); it does not transmit the actual confidential message payload itself over the quantum channel. Furthermore, QKD mandatorily requires an authenticated classical communication channel alongside the quantum channel—first to perform basis reconciliation (sifting), error estimation, and privacy amplification during key agreement, and subsequently to transmit the encrypted message ciphertext (encrypted using the QKD-derived symmetric key via AES-256 or a One-Time Pad).

Statement 2 is incorrect. Classical public-key cryptography (such as RSA) relies on the hardness of prime factorization, while Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) relies on mathematical problems believed to resist quantum attacks (such as high-dimensional lattice problems like Learning With Errors). In contrast, QKD offers information-theoretic security grounded strictly in the fundamental laws of quantum mechanics (Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle, quantum superposition collapse, and the No-Cloning Theorem), entirely independent of an adversary's computational power.

Statement 3 is incorrect on two physical grounds. First, QKD does not physically block an eavesdropper (Eve) from tapping the fiber or intercepting photons; rather, any measurement attempt by Eve irreversibly disturbs the quantum states and spikes the Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER), alerting Alice and Bob to discard the compromised key before any sensitive data is sent. Second, in accordance with the No-Communication Theorem and special relativity, entanglement cannot transmit classical information or usable cryptographic keys faster than the speed of light, because Alice and Bob must still exchange measurement basis information over a classical channel limited by the speed of light.

ref: TEC India Standard on Quantum Key Distribution; Bennett & Brassard (BB84 Protocol)

stem: With reference to long-distance Quantum Communication networks comparing terrestrial fiber-optic links and free-space satellite links, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In terrestrial silica fiber-optic cables, single-photon signals suffer exponential absorption and scattering losses over distance, limiting direct point-to-point fiber QKD without intermediate nodes to a few hundred kilometers.

2. To extend terrestrial QKD across thousands of kilometers, standard erbium-doped optical amplifiers and classical repeaters are placed periodically along the fiber to boost weak single-photon signals without disturbing their quantum superposition.

3. Free-space satellite-based QKD overcomes the range limits of terrestrial fibers because photons travelling between an orbiting satellite and ground stations propagate mostly through the vacuum of space, encountering atmospheric attenuation and turbulence only in the lowest layer of the path.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Classical optical amplifiers cannot be used in quantum communication networks because cloning or measuring-and-regenerating a photon destroys its quantum state; therefore, intercontinental QKD relies either on trusted relay nodes, experimental entanglement-swapping quantum repeaters, or free-space Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite links where vacuum propagation minimizes photon loss.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Even at optimal telecom wavelengths (1550 nm), standard silica optical fibers exhibit an attenuation loss of approximately 0.16 to 0.20 dB/km due to Rayleigh scattering and material absorption. Because QKD relies on single photons (or weak coherent pulses), exponential photon loss reduces the secret key rate to near zero beyond roughly 100–400 km in commercial point-to-point terrestrial deployments.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Standard erbium-doped fiber amplifiers (EDFAs) work via stimulated emission (which inherently clones photons and injects spontaneous emission noise), and classical optoelectronic repeaters measure and regenerate bit streams. Due to the No-Cloning Theorem, applying a classical amplifier or repeater to a qubit immediately collapses its superposition or breaks entanglement. Extending terrestrial QKD currently requires either physically secured 'Trusted Nodes' (where keys are decrypted into classical form and re-encrypted) or dedicated Quantum Repeaters based on quantum memories and entanglement swapping.

Statement 3 is correct. In satellite-to-ground free-space QKD, the effective thickness of the dense lower atmosphere is only equivalent to about 10–15 km of horizontal air at sea level, while the remaining hundreds of kilometers of the optical path lie in the near-vacuum of space where absorption and scattering are virtually zero, experiencing only geometric beam diffraction (inverse-square scaling rather than exponential fiber attenuation).

ref: ISRO Free-Space Quantum Communication Demonstration Notes; National Quantum Mission Vertical on Quantum Communications

stem: Consider the following computational stages involved in the end-to-end training and alignment lifecycle of a modern instruction-following Large Language Model (LLM):
items: 1. Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on curated, high-quality prompt-response demonstration pairs
2. Sub-word Tokenization and numerical vector embedding of a massive raw unlabeled text corpus
3. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) using a trained reward model to align outputs with safety and human preferences
4. Self-Supervised Pre-training via autoregressive next-token prediction across billions of neural parameters to construct the foundational Base Model
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of executing these stages from start to finish?
core: Developing a frontier conversational LLM follows a strict four-stage pipeline: first converting raw text into discrete sub-word tokens and vector embeddings (Stage 2), second executing compute-intensive Self-Supervised Pre-training to build a general Base Model (Stage 4), third applying Supervised Fine-Tuning on curated instruction-response pairs (Stage 1), and finally executing RLHF/DPO preference alignment for safety and helpfulness (Stage 3).

exp.why: Item 1 (Supervised Fine-Tuning / SFT) is the THIRD chronological stage. Once the pre-trained Base Model has learned general linguistic, factual, and reasoning patterns, it still behaves merely as a document auto-completer rather than an assistant. SFT trains the Base Model on a smaller, meticulously curated dataset of human-written instruction-response pairs so it learns to follow user commands and adopt a conversational format.

Item 2 (Sub-word Tokenization and Embedding) is the FIRST chronological stage. Because neural networks can only perform matrix mathematics on numbers, raw scraped text must first be segmented into discrete sub-word units (using algorithms such as Byte-Pair Encoding or WordPiece), mapped to integer token IDs, and projected into high-dimensional dense numerical vectors (embeddings) before any neural training can occur.

Item 3 (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback / RLHF) is the FOURTH and final chronological stage. After SFT, human evaluators rank multiple candidate responses generated by the SFT model to train a separate Reward Model (or directly optimize policies via PPO/DPO). This stage suppresses toxic hallucinations, enforces safety guardrails, and aligns the model's tone and helpfulness with human preferences.

Item 4 (Self-Supervised Pre-training) is the SECOND chronological stage, immediately following tokenization. Using the tokenized corpus, the Transformer architecture undergoes massive self-supervised training—requiring no manual human labels—by repeatedly predicting the next token in trillions of text sequences and updating billions of weights via backpropagation. Inverting SFT/RLHF before Self-Supervised Pre-training (as in options B and D) is architecturally impossible because fine-tuning and alignment require an already pre-trained foundational knowledge base.

ref: IndiaAI Mission Technical Report on Foundational Models; Vaswani et al. & Ouyang et al. (InstructGPT Pipeline)
